video_title: Value Stocks Set To Outperform Tech Into The End Of Year? | Lance Roberts
gist: Lance Roberts (RIA Advisors) explains why RIA rotated from growth to value into Q4 2026, citing midterm-year seasonality (~6.6% avg Q4), record upward guidance, and equal-weight lag, with falling oil as the catalyst for rate-sensitive sectors. He argues 5.3% 10-year yields reflect growth plus inflation rather than deficits, rejects calls for 7-8% secular yields, and lays out how to use individual bonds and munis (tax-equivalent yield, revenue-backed issues) while watching CCC credit spreads.

insights.claim: RIA Advisors did a full portfolio rebalance into Q4, shifting from growth to value because of widening divergences between overbought mega-cap growth and beaten-down value/small-cap factors.
insights.speaker: Lance Roberts
insights.so_what: Manager is actively positioning for value to outperform tech into year-end.

insights.claim: Factor rotation work shows S&P growth, mega-cap growth, ARK disruptive tech and semiconductors as the most overbought, while developed international and small-cap value are starting to gain traction, though the rotation is still early 'nibbling'.
insights.speaker: Lance Roberts
insights.so_what: Early rotation signal out of high-beta tech is emerging but unconfirmed.

insights.claim: A drop in oil back to around $80 would ease inflation pressure, pull yields lower, and fuel a rotation trade into rate-sensitive sectors such as REITs and utilities.
insights.speaker: Lance Roberts
insights.so_what: Oil is the swing catalyst for the rate-sensitive value trade.
insights.quote: if we get oil prices back down at the $80 range, we should see a decent rotation into some of those more interest rate sensitive sectors, REITs, utilities

insights.claim: Financials, real estate and industrials are heavily deviated below their long-term means, which typically sets up at least a decent trade into year-end, but Roberts frames it as a trade, not a long-term hold.
insights.speaker: Lance Roberts
insights.so_what: Mean-reversion trade in laggard sectors, not a secular call.
insights.quote: Not necessarily a long-term hold, but at least for now, kind of a decent trade setup.

insights.claim: The cap-weighted S&P 500 set an all-time high this week but, excluding a four-day spike, has been essentially flat for six months, with the 20- and 50-day moving averages sitting on top of each other as support.
insights.speaker: Lance Roberts
insights.so_what: Index strength masks a range-bound market with tight support.

insights.claim: A large performance gap between the S&P 500 equal-weight and cap-weight indices triggered a buy signal for RIA, prompting the rebalance toward value.
insights.speaker: Lance Roberts
insights.so_what: Equal-weight vs cap-weight spread is the trigger for the rotation trade.

insights.claim: Early turns are visible in financials, industrials and utilities, sectors that sold off on the roughly one-month spike in interest rates.
insights.speaker: Lance Roberts
insights.so_what: Watch these sectors for confirmation of rotation.

insights.claim: Roberts expects the cap-weighted index may go nowhere into year-end while equal-weight, small- and mid-cap indices could do better, so his highest-confidence call is on the broader market rather than the headline index.
insights.speaker: Lance Roberts
insights.so_what: Breadth, not the headline index, is where upside is expected.

insights.claim: RIA took profits in tech winners such as AMD and Nvidia back to target weights, harvested tax losses in short-duration bonds and some rate-hit small caps (to rebuy after the wash-sale window), and added Berkshire Hathaway B shares, utilities, JPMorgan and Goldman Sachs.
insights.speaker: Lance Roberts
insights.so_what: Concrete positioning: trimming semis, adding value financials and utilities.

insights.claim: Banks face a mixed rate impact: higher yields hurt bond-portfolio values (as with Silicon Valley Bank) and improve loan margins, but loan volume is drying up, with 7.5% mortgages and slowing commercial lending, while private credit demand remains strong.
insights.speaker: Lance Roberts
insights.so_what: Bank upside depends on loan volume holding up despite high rates.

insights.claim: In midterm years where Q1 was negative and Q2 rose more than 10%, the S&P 500's Q4 (Oct 1-Dec 31) has averaged about a 6.6% return; 16 of the last 19 midterm years were positive.
insights.speaker: Lance Roberts
insights.so_what: Seasonal tailwind favors a year-end rally, with averages masking dispersion.
insights.quote: out of the last 19 midterm years 16 were positive three were negative

insights.claim: Sentiment is a contrarian tailwind: the CNN Fear & Greed index is in fear, retail is largely on the sidelines, and CTAs are underweight equity exposure.
insights.speaker: Lance Roberts
insights.so_what: Under-positioning leaves room for a chase higher.

insights.claim: Buybacks returning from their blackout window add liquidity (the blackout was not a removal of liquidity, just an absence of addition), and overall market liquidity is plentiful.
insights.speaker: Lance Roberts
insights.so_what: Corporate bid returns into earnings season.

insights.claim: Earnings season enters on strong footing, with 72 companies raising full-year guidance versus 44 at or below, which Roberts calls a record number of higher guidance revisions.
insights.speaker: Lance Roberts
insights.so_what: Positive guidance skew supports the year-end rally thesis.
insights.quote: we've already had 72 companies report higher guidance for this year versus 44 uh reporting at or lower guidance for this year

insights.claim: Historically the S&P's 12-month post-midterm return is positive under any government combination, highest (13-17%) under gridlock, about 7% with an opposite-party Congress, and lowest with a Democratic Congress and Republican president, which polls currently suggest.
insights.speaker: Lance Roberts
insights.so_what: Polling points to the weakest historical political configuration for 2027 returns.

insights.claim: A Democratic sweep of Congress would raise the odds of higher taxes and more restrictive market regulation, explaining historically lower returns, so the November 3 midterms will heavily shape how year-end plays out.
insights.speaker: Lance Roberts
insights.so_what: Election outcome is a key risk to the year-end call.

themes.theme: Bond yields: what sets them and where they go

insights.claim: The 10-year Treasury yield is stuck around 5.2-5.3%, and this week's 10-year and 30-year auctions were very strong with heavy foreign buying, even though media coverage focuses only on weak auctions.
insights.speaker: Lance Roberts
insights.so_what: Demand for duration at these yields is robust, countering the fiscal-crisis narrative.

insights.claim: Roberts' yield model: real growth (Atlanta Fed GDPNow still near 4% for Q3, down from about 6%) plus about 3% inflation from strong nominal growth and oil, plus a roughly 1% term premium set by inflation expectations, gives about 5.3%, exactly where the 10-year trades.
insights.speaker: Lance Roberts
insights.so_what: Yields are explained by growth and inflation, not fiscal fear.

insights.claim: Roberts argues debts and deficits do not drive interest rates higher; they are disinflationary over time because they erode economic growth, and rates fell from 9% in 1994 even as debt rose from $9 trillion to $18 trillion between the Obama and Trump inaugurations.
insights.speaker: Lance Roberts
insights.so_what: Directly rebuts the consensus fiscal-dominance case for higher yields.
insights.quote: debts and deficits are disinflationary over time because it erodess economic activity and economic growth

insights.claim: Roberts rejects banking analyst Chris Whalen's view of secularly rising yields to 7-8%+ for generations, arguing such rates would destroy the economy and therefore cannot persist.
insights.speaker: Lance Roberts
insights.so_what: Debate between secular bond bears and RIA's disinflation view frames duration risk.

insights.claim: Stripping out AI-related capex spending, the US economy is close to flat, with consumer demand destruction already occurring; once capex ends within about two years, the real economy will drive yields lower.
insights.speaker: Lance Roberts
insights.so_what: Capex cycle end is the catalyst for lower yields.
insights.quote: if you strip out the capex spending in this economy, we are close to flat

insights.claim: Historically, whenever the 10-year yield has been three standard deviations above its monthly moving average it has marked the peak in rates, coinciding with economic events such as the Asian contagion, dot-com crisis, financial crisis and pandemic.
insights.speaker: Lance Roberts
insights.so_what: Extreme deviation in yields signals an approaching top.

insights.claim: Current yields are a normalization from artificial ZIRP/QE suppression for 15 years, so 5% is about the historical average since the 1970s rather than a crisis signal.
insights.speaker: Lance Roberts
insights.so_what: Reframes high yields as normal pricing, not fiscal breakdown.

insights.claim: Without the Iran war oil shock, the US would likely be experiencing disinflation now, which means bonds locked at today's yields would see rising real yields as inflation falls.
insights.speaker: Adam Taggart
insights.so_what: Locking in nominal yields now could deliver improving real returns.

insights.claim: Roberts says the only reasons to own bonds are guaranteed income, lower portfolio volatility and guaranteed return of principal; if you do not need all three, do not buy bonds.
insights.speaker: Lance Roberts
insights.so_what: Bond buying should be driven by function, not rate forecasts.

insights.claim: RIA bought a 5-year Treasury at 5% and is buying 5-, 7- and 10-year duration, while expected real equity returns over the next decade from current valuations are roughly -2% to +2%, so a 5.3% 10-year Treasury nearly doubles expected stock returns.
insights.speaker: Lance Roberts
insights.so_what: Valuation math favors adding duration now for goal-based investors.
insights.quote: expected real returns on stocks is going to be somewhere between -2 and 2% over the next decade

insights.claim: Bonds now supply about 53% of the return a typical investor needs to reach their goal versus about 12% three years ago.
insights.speaker: Lance Roberts
insights.so_what: Higher yields let retirees de-risk equity exposure.

insights.claim: Bond ETFs never mature and are purely a bet on rate direction, so investors needing capital preservation should own individual bonds held to maturity; mortgage-backed securities are worse because principal amortizes away.
insights.speaker: Lance Roberts
insights.so_what: Vehicle choice matters: ETFs do not deliver principal protection.

insights.claim: Only yield to maturity matters, not the coupon: paying 107 for a bond maturing at 100 locks in a 7% principal loss offset by coupon.
insights.speaker: Lance Roberts
insights.so_what: Investors should evaluate bonds on YTM and real yield.

insights.claim: Rebalancing from equity gains into bonds raises portfolio income over time, which is how a balanced portfolio adjusts bond income for inflation even though a fixed coupon does not.
insights.speaker: Lance Roberts
insights.so_what: Rebalancing discipline turns equity gains into growing income.

insights.claim: Older investors hold record equity allocations after ZIRP conditioning; with the TINA-to-TIGA shift ('there is a good alternative'), now is the time to normalize toward bonds.
insights.speaker: Adam Taggart
insights.so_what: Large reallocation from equities to bonds could be a flow headwind for stocks.

insights.claim: Flows into bonds versus equities have been very large this year, and if that 'good alternative' extraction of capital from equities accelerates it becomes a problem for stock markets.
insights.speaker: Lance Roberts
insights.so_what: Monitor bond-vs-equity flow acceleration as a market risk.

themes.theme: Credit spreads and the next bear market

insights.claim: Credit spreads are widening only in CCC and C-rated debt; BBB, A, BB and single-B spreads are not moving, and the rate of change is not yet a spike that signals trouble.
insights.speaker: Lance Roberts
insights.so_what: No systemic credit stress yet despite the junk-tier blowout.

insights.claim: Credit spreads are the best leading indicator for markets; a cascade of widening up the quality ladder, along with flows from corporates into Treasuries like in 2008, would signal cutting equity risk.
insights.speaker: Lance Roberts
insights.so_what: Defines the specific trigger to de-risk.

insights.claim: Higher rates pressure small and mid-cap companies more because they lack cash flows to service debt and face refinancing issues.
insights.speaker: Lance Roberts
insights.so_what: Small-cap value upside is constrained while rates stay high.

insights.claim: RIA's long-term thesis is a secular bear market likely in the 2030s rather than the next couple of years, during which bonds outperform; at the bottom they would sell bonds and go 100% equities, as they shifted equity into Treasuries after a June 2008 head-and-shoulders neckline break.
insights.speaker: Lance Roberts
insights.so_what: Cycle playbook: Treasuries into the bust, equities and distressed credit out of it.

insights.claim: In the next crisis, flight to Treasuries will blow out corporate and municipal yields, creating rare opportunities like Exxon Mobil bonds at 80 cents on the dollar as in 2008.
insights.speaker: Lance Roberts
insights.so_what: Keep dry powder for distressed investment-grade credit.

insights.claim: The paradox Steven Bavaria highlights: investors who refuse high-yield debt still buy the same companies' equity, which is junior and riskier.
insights.speaker: Adam Taggart
insights.so_what: Risk perception is inconsistent across the capital structure.

insights.claim: Gen Z has been conditioned that markets always rebound quickly, driving gambling-like behavior via Polymarket, Kalshi, leveraged ETFs and 0DTE options, a moral hazard created by the Fed put.
insights.speaker: Lance Roberts
insights.so_what: Speculative excess is vulnerable if the Fed does not rescue the next correction.
insights.quote: Question is what happens if the Fed doesn't step in on the next correction?

insights.claim: Higher yields have a positive side for savers and housing affordability as they clear malinvestment, though big banks still pay near-zero, with JPMorgan money-market interest at zero.
insights.speaker: Adam Taggart
insights.so_what: Banks profit on deposit spreads while savers sweep cash elsewhere.

insights.claim: Munis should be judged only on tax-equivalent yield: if a 3% tax-free muni compares to a 4% after-tax Treasury, buy the Treasury and pay the tax.
insights.speaker: Lance Roberts
insights.so_what: Tax aversion leads investors into lower real returns.

insights.claim: Muni spreads versus tax-equivalent Treasury yields are currently too tight to justify the risk; they will widen in the next downturn when weaker municipalities default, and that is when Roberts would buy.
insights.speaker: Lance Roberts
insights.so_what: Wait for a credit event to add munis.

insights.claim: Prefer revenue-backed munis (toll roads, school districts, MUD utility districts) and insured issues over general obligations of fiscally stressed cities like San Francisco or hospital bonds, which tend to go bankrupt.
insights.speaker: Lance Roberts
insights.so_what: Specific credit-screen for muni selection.

insights.claim: Quality short-duration munis are scarce for individuals because muni funds absorb new issues immediately, leaving retail with leftover lower-quality paper; advisers buying $20-30M blocks get better access and pricing.
insights.speaker: Lance Roberts
insights.so_what: Muni market structure disadvantages retail buyers.

insights.claim: Tax-free munis belong in taxable accounts, not IRAs or Roth IRAs, and residents of no-income-tax states like Nevada, Texas and Florida can buy munis from any state.
insights.speaker: Lance Roberts
insights.so_what: Account location and residency drive muni value.
